body.narrative:
## Running the system
Atlas contains 6 assets and 1 edge, so its operational shape is sparse. The 4 devices and 1 project are the counted non-domain asset classes, and the 1 domain supplies the only edge context. The 1 SERVES edge is the only counted relationship; it does not imply multiple service bindings because worker_wiring.service_binding_target=0. worker_wiring.total=0 tracks 0 workers, with all invocation counts at 0: served=0, workers_dev=0, cron=0, service_binding_target=0. unwired_workers=0 makes the no-invocation signal 0, not a worker-usage verdict. projects_no_repo=1 says 1 of 1 projects lacks a repo link; the gap is 1 link, not a worker count. data_stores=[] and stale=0 show 0 data stores and 0 stale items, so 0 store capacity is visible and 0 decay is visible.

## Security
curated_targets=0 against 1 domain yields a 0-of-1 ratio. The curated-target ratio is 0 curated_targets to 1 total domain. auth_curation_gaps=1 is the security signal: the 1 served domain has no curated auth-boundary target. The 1 gap is still in the hourly hygiene sweep; the 1 is a curation gap, not a scan gap. For auth-bearing surfaces, the 1 gap means 1 domain needs 1 curated boundary; for static surfaces, 1 domain still needs 1 classification, not necessarily auth. stale=0 adds 0 extra freshness risk to the 1-domain gap.

## How things interconnect
blast_zones=[] and data_stores=[] show 0 counted blast zones and 0 counted data stores, so there are 0 top zones and 0 owned records to name. edge_census has 1 SERVES edge and 0 counted RUNS_ON or CALLS edges, so the fan-out and fan-in count is 0. With 1 edge across 6 assets, the 1 visible relationship is the full dependency map. If the 1 edge changed, 1 counted connection would disappear, but blast_zones=0 quantifies downstream record loss as 0. RUNS_ON=0, CALLS=0, and blast_zones=0 support 0 concentration-risk conclusion.

chain.name: System Prompt
chain.role: The constitutional layer — the five constitutional rules, the ONE output format, verification doctrine, security protocol, hard prohibitions. Highest authority; wins every conflict.

summary.markdown: This file is the constitutional system prompt that defines who the DA is, the single output format every response must follow, the verification doctrine (no done-claims without tool evidence), and five hard prohibitions that override every other rule in the system. It loads every turn as an appended system prompt, meaning it is always in context and never needs explicit invocation. If it vanished, the DA would lose its identity voice, its mandatory response structure would collapse into freeform output, the verification gate would have no authority to refuse "should work" claims, and the five constitutional rules that win all conflicts would simply not exist — effectively removing the system's spine.

chain.name: CLAUDE.md
chain.role: The routing table — where everything lives. Pulls the always-on @-imports: architecture summary, TELOS, principal + DA identity, projects, operational rules.

summary.markdown: CLAUDE.md is the global entry point for the entire LifeOS harness — on every conversation turn, Claude Code auto-loads it and resolves all `@`-imports, injecting the architecture summary, principal identity, DA identity, TELOS, projects, and operational rules directly into the model's context before any user message is seen. It also functions as a routing table: a single map of every LifeOS component on disk, so the AI knows where to find the Algorithm, Cortex, Pulse, Ledger, and every other subsystem when it needs to read or edit one. If this file vanished, the AI would wake up with no identity, no life goals, no memory of who it's assisting, and no knowledge of where anything lives — the Algorithm would still "think" but with no principal to think for and no system to operate within. The file also encodes a priority rule: when CLAUDE.md and the system prompt disagree, the system prompt wins, preventing any local override of constitutional constraints.

chain.name: Operational Rules
chain.role: Principal-specific operating rules — model selection, versioning, deploy doctrine, design variety, releases, autonomy boundaries. @-imported every turn.

summary.markdown: This file defines the principal-specific rules that the system prompt cannot carry generically — model tier assignments (MAX for judgment, HIGH for execution, MEDIUM for trivial legs), deployment conventions, tool preferences, and the security allowlist for trusted channels and authorization. It loads into context every single turn via @-import from CLAUDE.md, so its contents are always live in the system prompt's reasoning window. The "Model selection" section is the most operationally load-bearing part: the system prompt, AlgorithmNudge, ModelRungGuard, and models.ts all read it to decide which model tier to route each work unit through. If the file vanished, the system would lose its tier-routing logic (falling back to running everything on the session's pinned model, losing cost/latency optimization), the security boundaries would have no target to resolve trusted senders or the work-repo carve-out against, and every consequential action would be permanently blocked at "ask first" with no path to authorization. It currently ships as an unedited template stub, so in its present state it contributes only the default model-tier semantics and a blank security allowlist.

chain.name: LoadContext hook
chain.role: SessionStart injection — builds the LifeOS dynamic context block (learning frames, active work, architecture pointers) the session opens with.

summary.markdown: On every new session start, this hook scans MEMORY/WORK directories (last 48h), relationship notes, learning/wisdom frames, and advisory digests, then emits a structured `<system-reminder>` block to stdout that Claude reads as its opening context — no user prompt required. It is blocking (execution completes before the session becomes interactive) and skips entirely for subagent contexts. If it vanished, Claude would open every session with no awareness of what you've been actively working on, what recent relationship opinions or failure patterns it should recall, or what the previous session's advisory review found — forcing you to manually re-orient the assistant at the start of each conversation.

chain.name: LoadMemory hook
chain.role: Every-prompt injection of the hot-layer memory files (PRINCIPAL_MEMORY, DA_MEMORY) so each turn sees current memory.

summary.markdown: On every user prompt, this hook reads the two hot-layer memory files from disk and injects them as a `<lifeos-memory>` context block so the CLI session sees the same memory the autonomic loop has been writing. It runs as a UserPromptSubmit hook, skips subagent invocations (they only see what their parent passed them), and on any error silently exits 0 rather than blocking the prompt. Without it, the principal's CLI session would be permanently memory-blind — the autonomic loop would keep curating PRINCIPAL_MEMORY and DA_MEMORY but only remote channels like iMessage and Siri would actually read them, creating a parity gap where the same person talks to two different states of knowledge depending on the channel. The files are capped at 48 entries and ~12K chars each, keeping injection cheap enough to fire on every turn without noticeable latency.

chain.name: The Algorithm (doctrine)
chain.role: The thinking loop itself — euphoric surprise as the target, the ISA as hill + instrument, the 16 done-claims with their teeth (HOOK/CHECK/SELF), the event nudge table, spend doctrine. Read at the start of any substantial run.

summary.markdown: This file is the Algorithm's core definition-of-done specification: it defines the thinking loop (conjecture/refutation against an ISA), states 16 completion claims with their enforcement teeth (HOOK, CHECK, or SELF), and sets the spend doctrine that intelligence and resources must scale to task difficulty. It loads as the first action on any substantial run, before any building begins, and its claims gate whether the run is allowed to close. Without it, the system loses its only mechanical enforcement of verification rigor — there would be no ISA scaffold requirement, no tool-evidence gate blocking premature closure, no class-sweep obligation, no ask-fidelity check, and no baseline-parity rule preventing silent regressions; the entire "proof over promise" discipline collapses back into soft judgment.

chain.name: Algorithm Changelog
chain.role: Every doctrine version's full history: what changed, why, migration and rollback recipes. Doctrine files stay lean; history lives here.

summary.markdown: This file stores the complete version history of the Algorithm doctrine — every patch, feature, and correction since the system began, along with migration steps and rollback recipes for each. It loads on demand and never executes code; its sole purpose is to keep the active doctrine file (`vX.Y.Z.md`) free of historical prose and incident narratives. Without it, each new doctrine version would either bloat the active file with change-log noise or leave no auditable trail of why a rule was added, what broke to motivate it, or how to undo it in one command.

chain.name: ISA Format Spec
chain.role: The contract for the Ideal State Artifact — section order, claim shapes, ID stability, the Splitting and Variation tests. The ISA is where 'done' gets written down before building.

summary.markdown: This is the authoritative format contract for the Ideal State Artifact — the single markdown document that each run produces to define what "done" means before any building starts. It loads during a run whenever ISA scaffolding, validation, or rendering occurs, and it governs everything downstream: section order, claim ID stability, the Splitting and Variation tests, dependency-edge syntax, verifier classes, and the complete set of fifteen-plus body sections. If it vanished, the parser (isa-utils), the gate (ISAGate), the frontier tool (IsaFrontier), Bunker's claim reader, and the renderer would each keep working mechanically against already-written code, but the shared contract that keeps them mutually consistent would be gone, so any future change to one component would silently desync the others. It is effectively the schema specification for the system's primary data artifact, and without it no one can authoritatively answer "is this ISA valid?" or "what does a new section need to look like?"

chain.name: ISA System doc
chain.role: How the ISA subsystem works end to end — lifecycle, homes (repo ISA vs MEMORY/WORK), sync to Pulse, resume semantics.

summary.markdown: This file is the conceptual foundation document for the ISA (Ideal State Articulation) — the central primitive that every other part of LifeOS exists to create, pursue, and verify. It defines what an ISA is, why it replaces specs/plans/PRDs, how Ideal State Criteria work as hard-to-vary claims, and how the ISA relates to the Algorithm (ISA is the hill, Algorithm is the climb). It loads on demand when an agent or user needs the full architectural reasoning behind ISA lifecycle, homes, sync, and resume semantics rather than just the format spec. If it vanished, agents would still have the mechanical format rules from ISAFormat.md but would lose the philosophical and design rationale that governs how to write good claims, handle fog, distinguish goal from ideal state, and know when to fix the ISA versus the code — leading to degraded articulation quality across every build.

chain.name: ISA skill
chain.role: The skill that scaffolds, interviews, scores completeness, reconciles, and appends to ISAs — the operational front door to the ISA system.

summary.markdown: This file is the operational interface for the Ideal State Artifact system — when invoked, it routes the user's intent (scaffold, interview, grill, check, reconcile, seed, or append) to the correct workflow file, first firing a voice notification via a local curl call, then generating or refining a locked seventeen-section document that hard-fixes what "done" means for a given piece of work. It loads on any ISA-related command and never runs in the background. If it vanished, the entire specification-and-verification backbone of the Algorithm system loses its only front door: no new ISAs get created, existing ones can't be scored for completeness, ephemeral feature slices can't be reconciled back to master, and the coverage gate that blocks premature completion evaporates — leaving agents to work against drift-prone, unstructured notions of "finished" with no shared source of truth across sessions.

chain.name: ISASync hook
chain.role: Mirrors every ISA write to the work registry (work.json) → Pulse. This write IS the run telemetry — claim 13's carrier.

summary.markdown: This hook fires on every Write, Edit, or Read targeting an ISA.md (or legacy PRD.md) file and is the single mechanism that registers a run into work.json, making it visible to every dashboard surface. On writes it parses the ISA's frontmatter, syncs it into the registry, derives the run's ascent state, repaints the terminal tab on phase transitions, and injects a verbatim phase-strip block into the model's context whenever the derived state changes so the model never has to compute its own status line. Read events are handled as heartbeats only — they bump lastToolActivity on the slug without mutating the ISA. On transition to COMPLETE it spawns ISARender to produce the HTML mirror. If this hook vanished, no run would ever appear on the board, no phase strips would reach the model, tabs would never change color, and the HTML mirrors would never generate.

chain.name: CheckpointPerISC hook
chain.role: Auto git-commit on every claim close (`[ ]`→`[x]`) — evidence trail per closed claim, part of claim 8's teeth.

summary.markdown: Fires after any Write or Edit tool touches an ISA.md file, parses the file for newly-checked criteria (`[ ]`→`[x]`), and for each newly-closed criterion stages only the files this run touched in every allowlisted git repo, producing one conventional commit per repo with the ISC ID, slug, and description as commit body. It runs synchronously inside the hook window with hard timeouts, uses a sidecar JSON state file to prevent double-commits, and refuses to act if the ISA frontmatter lacks a parseable `started` timestamp so it can distinguish this session's work from another concurrent session's dirty files. If this file vanished, the Algorithm would lose its automatic evidence trail — closed claims would have no per-repo commit anchoring the exact moment of completion, making post-hoc audit of "what changed when claim N closed" impossible to reconstruct from git history alone.

chain.name: ISARenderOnStop hook
chain.role: Re-renders edited ISAs at end-of-turn so the HTML mirror stays current with the artifact.

summary.markdown: Fires at turn-end (Stop event) and spawns background ISARender.ts processes for every ISA that was edited during the turn, regenerating each one's HTML mirror so the rendered artifact stays in sync with the source. It enforces a doctrinal gate that refuses to re-render an ISA that has never reached `phase: complete` at least once — this prevents constant remaking of documents still in active first-authoring — but catches the edge case of resumed or pre-convention ISAs by inspecting frontmatter when no HTML sibling exists yet. It reads the list of edited paths from a per-session state file written by ISASync.hook.ts, clears that file immediately after processing, and logs render/skip outcomes to an observability JSONL. Renders are spawned detached and unref'd so the hook itself never blocks the Stop event beyond a trivial filesystem read. If this hook vanished, ISA.html mirrors would silently go stale after any edit to a completed document, breaking the mirror convention that downstream consumers (browsing, exporting, cross-referencing) rely on.

chain.name: AlgorithmNudge hook
chain.role: The live event layer — deterministic nudges fired at the moment they're answerable: skill-routing, late-ISA, depth directives (always-on); probe-failure, mid-run messages, spend checks (run-scoped).

summary.markdown: This is the Algorithm's real-time feedback loop: it watches every prompt and every tool result, checks cheap state (did tool calls pile up without an ISA edit? did a capability the Doctor knows is broken just fail? did a destructive infra command run?), and injects a single one-line advisory question into the conversation at the exact moment it can be answered. It fires on UserPromptSubmit (skill-routing, depth directives, design-class, exec-delegation) and on PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure (stale-ISA, late-ISA, capability fix, destructive-infra), maintaining a per-session JSON that tracks tool-call counts, run state, and cooldowns. It never blocks execution and never makes an inference call—it is purely deterministic pattern-matching against observable state the model cannot see from inside its own context (an unwritten ISA, a manifest-known-broken capability, a resource that owned DNS records it just deleted). Without it, the Algorithm's doctrine ("design the thing natively," "dispatch a rung down," "re-list from the authority post-op") exists only as prose the model ignores under load; the nudge is the mechanism that converts written rules into in-the-moment questions at the precise turn where they change behavior.

chain.name: VerificationGate hook
chain.role: Mechanical teeth for claim 8 — no claim closes without tool evidence of the right modality; web/UI claims need a real browser, appearance claims need viewed pixels.

summary.markdown: This hook fires on Stop, reads the AI's closing message for verification or publicity claims (e.g., "the site is live," "the login flow works," "v7.23.2 is public"), then scans the turn's actual tool-call transcript for evidence matching the claim's modality — a real probe for deploys, a rendered pixel view for appearance claims, a pushed public surface for publicity claims. If a blocking-type claim exists but the required evidence is absent or stale, the hook blocks the stop and forces the AI to either produce the evidence or retract the claim; it fails open on any parse error so it never prevents a legitimate stop. It is the system's only mechanical defense against the AI confidently asserting completion or public visibility at the exact moment a human would rely on that assertion; removing it reintroduces the fabrication class (three fabricated publicity claims in one session) that originally motivated its creation.

chain.name: StopGates hook
chain.role: The ONE Stop-event gate runner — merges the per-turn gate spawns into a single process reading stdin once; each gate file stays owner of its logic.

summary.markdown: This is the sole Stop-event gate runner: at every turn end it reads stdin once and sequentially evaluates seven quality gates (format structure, claim-vs-evidence verification, ISA-close staleness, ISA-fold detection, ISA structural granularity, deploy registration, and writing audit), emitting the first block decision it encounters or silently passing if all gates clear. It fires on every Stop event, meaning it runs after every single agent turn regardless of what the agent was doing. Without it, none of the Algorithm's enforcement teeth would fire at turn boundaries — stale ISA state, unverified completion claims, format violations, and unregistered production deploys would all go unchecked. Each gate's logic lives in its own file; this hook is purely the orchestration and fail-open wrapper, guaranteeing exit 0 so a gate crash never breaks the harness itself.

chain.name: FormatGate hook
chain.role: Deterministic Stop-hook teeth for the ONE output format — banner first, closer last, hook-fed memory lines echoed verbatim.

summary.markdown: On every turn end (Stop), this hook inspects the final assistant message for four structural rules: LifeOS banner as first line, 🗣️ closer as last line, presence of memory/system echo lines when a delta arrived that turn, and no more than two em-dashes in prose. It does not block or re-emit anything — violations are logged as `decision:"flag"` entries to `format-gate.jsonl` and the hook returns null, a deliberate downgrade from its earlier blocking behavior which caused duplicated output. It fails open on any error, skips when `stop_hook_active` is true to avoid loops, and strips code blocks and blockquotes before counting em-dashes so only authored prose is judged. Without this file you lose all format-drift telemetry and the feedback signal that tunes the DriftReminder nudge, but no functional path in the Algorithm system breaks since nothing downstream consumes the gate's return value.

chain.name: SpendAuditor hook
chain.role: Outcome-side spend verification (claim 15) — catches the heavy ask answered inline with zero capability use and no stated reason.

summary.markdown: After each assistant turn completes, this hook reads the session's state files to decide whether the response warrants a post-hoc effort audit — it triggers if AlgorithmNudge fired a depth signal this session, if the session shows zero Skill/Agent use against a prompt ≥200 characters, or if a work-registry item just hit "complete." When eligible, the hot path (<20 ms) writes a timestamp to a small state file and spawns a detached, unref'd background worker that reads the last 800 KB of the transcript, extracts the user ask and the assistant answer as gists, builds a capability trace, and calls the Inference CLI at low level to judge whether spend matched the ask. The verdict is appended to spend-audit.jsonl, and any underspend verdict at confidence ≥0.6 is also copied into capability-incidents.jsonl with a "spend-auditor" attribution so the RunCalibration harness and incident dashboards can track it. If this file vanished, the system would lose its only outcome-side depth verification — AlgorithmNudge would still catch depth signals at prompt time, but there would be no mechanism to detect or log the specific failure mode of a heavy ask answered inline with zero capability use, and the capability-incidents feed would lose a major source of confirmed underspend cases.

chain.name: WritingGate hook
chain.role: Publication gate — prose authored for the principal that will be published must pass the _WRITING audit + a real Pangram run, SHA-verified; typing the audit line without running the tool does not pass.

summary.markdown: When the assistant finishes a response containing outbound prose for the principal (a sponsored LinkedIn post, a blog draft, marketing copy), this Stop hook inspects the message for publication signals — a `#ad` caption, a hashtag cluster, a "Here's the post:" label, or blog frontmatter — and checks whether a real Pangram AI-detector run was logged this turn whose content SHA matches a deliverable block in the response. A typed `✍️ WRITING-AUDIT:` citation alone is never sufficient; the gate requires cryptographic proof the tool actually ran on this text. Strong signals with no verified run produce a `decision:block` that forces the assistant to re-run the audit before the response reaches the user; weak or ambiguous signals only log telemetry. On installs without a Pangram API key the hook degrades to telemetry instead of creating an unsatisfiable infinite loop. If removed, authored content would ship to the principal's public channels with no enforcement that the writing audit and AI detector ever ran, re-enabling the exact failure that motivated the file's creation.

chain.name: DriftReminder hook
chain.role: Voice/format drift nudge — flags when output slides away from the DA voice contract so the next turn corrects.

summary.markdown: On every user prompt it reads the previous response from disk, measures it against the LifeOS format contract (banner, closer, em-dash cap, line budget, banned words), and injects a one-line "FORMAT CONTRACT" string into the model's context that states this turn's line cap, the structural rules, and what specifically the last response broke — or confirms it was clean. It runs pre-generation, which is the key distinction from the old FormatGate that fired after output was already visible and could only block, forcing a wasteful re-emit. If it vanished the system would lose its only pre-write shape enforcement, and the measured drift rate would revert to the 61–91% daily violation level seen during the 19-day window when FormatGate was observation-only. It never blocks a prompt; any internal error exits 0 silently.

chain.name: Philosophy
chain.role: Why the system works this way — Deutsch epistemology, hard-to-vary claims, ideal-state prompting, the bitter-lesson stance on scaffolding.

summary.markdown: This file is the system's epistemological constitution — it defines what counts as a legitimate constraint versus cuttable scaffolding (the BPE taxonomy: safety-gates, verified-gotchas, tool-contracts, output-format-contracts) and articulates why verification, not procedure, is the core mechanism of the Algorithm. It loads on demand only, when the system needs to justify a design choice, write release notes, or adjudicate whether a skill body is ideal-state prompting or bitter-pill engineering. Without it, the system has no canonical test for the single most consequential editorial question in the repo — "would a smarter model make this rule unnecessary?" — and the line between architecture and choreography in every prompt, skill, and workflow becomes a matter of personal judgment rather than a shared, falsifiable standard.

chain.name: Verification Doctrine
chain.role: The ONE home of the six incident-derived verification rules (modality fidelity, defer-never-substitute, appearance ≠ existence, reproduce-before-fixing, temporal fidelity, restore-parity). Cites incidents by INC-ID.

summary.markdown: This file is the single canonical home of seven verification rules distilled from real incidents, defining what counts as valid proof for claims about web output, deployed infrastructure, and cache-dependent behavior. It loads on demand whenever the Algorithm must verify appearance, liveness, deployment, or propagation, and is mechanically enforced by VerificationGate.hook.ts (which blocks false "works/verified" claims at stop by grading actual tool calls in the transcript) and AlgorithmNudge.hook.ts (which fires ownership-enumeration and baseline-flow checks before any destructive infra deletion). Without it, the enforcement hooks have no rulebook to grade against, and agents regress to substituting weak proxies—curls, DOM reads, single cold probes, cached 200s—for real evidence, which is exactly the failure pattern every rule was written to prevent.

chain.name: Incidents
chain.role: The self-improvement loop's evidence base — one INC-YYYYMMDD-<slug>.md per verified LifeOS failure, cited by ID from rules and doctrine; narratives live here and only here.

chain.name: Self-Healing
chain.role: Where a new rule or fix structurally lives — hooks for enforcement, CLAUDE.md for routing, skills for domain behavior, KNOWLEDGE for facts. Fix the system, not your notes.
chain.loaded: On demand (encoding a learning / degraded state)

summary.markdown: This file is the routing table that decides where a new rule, fix, or learning should be structurally encoded in the LifeOS system — hooks for checkable gates, CLAUDE.md for operational preferences, skills for domain behavior, KNOWLEDGE for facts — and it explicitly blocks the default reflex of writing a memo or a new hook as visible proof of remediation. It loads on demand when the system encounters a recurring failure or degraded state, serving as the decision framework for that patch. It also specifies the autonomic nightly pipeline (RecurrenceLedger → failing-fixture draft → human/agent fix → green-gated promotion into the blocking regression corpus) that automates the last mile from detection to permanent regression without ever letting a model write code to an enforcement surface. Without it, the system loses its structured "fix the system, not your notes" doctrine and defaults to accumulating behavioral memos that require future sessions to remember to consult them, breaking the self-healing loop that makes rules structurally enforced from the moment they're encoded.

chain.name: Operational Rules Expanded
chain.role: The mechanics behind every operational rule — full rationale, incident history, procedures, same section names as the operative core. Read when a rule fires and you need the how.

chain.name: Writing Style Backstop
chain.role: The complete voice doctrine — ban lists, banned rhythms, the pre-emit checks, long-form exemplars. Loaded when auditing writing or a drift flag fires.

summary.markdown: This file is the DA's full voice enforcement reference — banned words, banned sentence patterns, a pre-send checklist, and the AI-detection posture the DA should adopt when auditing its own output. It loads only on demand: when a drift flag fires, when the DA reviews its own writing for violations, or when it's uncertain whether a construction is permitted. Without it, the system loses its expanded style doctrine, leaving only the abbreviated rules in DA_IDENTITY.md; drift corrections would have no reference to check against, and the DA would silently regress into banned tics, consultant register, and hedged claims.

When a message arrives, the system first loads its rules, identity, memory, and current work. It then treats the turn as either a quick answer or real work; there is no separate mode menu. A quick answer gets a plain response. Real work creates an ISA — a written definition of “done” made of testable claims — and the run climbs against those claims. Nothing is called done until a tool proves it: a test, a diff, a browser check, or another artifact the system can point at.

## Every turn — what loads before the first token and what wins conflicts.

Before the first token, `LIFEOS/LIFEOS_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md` supplies the constitutional rules and response shape. `CLAUDE.md` routes identity, projects, and operational rules; the session and prompt hooks (`hooks/LoadContext.hook.ts`, `hooks/LoadMemory.hook.ts`, `hooks/DriftReminder.hook.ts`) supply work, memory, and the format contract. If those files disagree, the system prompt wins.

## When work is real — how a run works: write done down, climb, close claims on evidence.

When the ask needs building or judgment, the run reads `LIFEOS/ALGORITHM/LATEST`, then the matching `v*.md` file. It writes done down in an ISA, usually via `skills/ISA/SKILL.md`, then works against those claims. Each claim names a probe that could prove it false. A claim closes only when that probe passes; `hooks/CheckpointPerISC.hook.ts` commits the close, and the ISA points at the proof.

## The teeth — hooks that block mechanically vs checks vs self-attestation; name the actual hook files.

Blocking gates run through `hooks/StopGates.hook.ts`; `hooks/VerificationGate.hook.ts` refuses a done claim when the actual tool calls lack the right kind of evidence. `hooks/ISAGate.hook.ts` blocks close on structural ISA mistakes. `hooks/AlgorithmNudge.hook.ts` and `hooks/SpendAuditor.hook.ts` only ask questions or record outcomes; they do not block. The rest is checks plus self-attestation, where the model judges itself and can be wrong.

## Where the rules live — which files carry what, so the reader knows what to edit to change behavior.

Behavior and response format live in `LIFEOS/LIFEOS_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md`; identity and voice live in `LIFEOS/USER/DIGITAL_ASSISTANT/DA_IDENTITY.md`. Routing lives in `CLAUDE.md`, while model choices and trusted channels live in `LIFEOS/USER/CONFIG/OPERATIONAL_RULES.md`. The loop lives in the current Algorithm file, the ISA shape in `LIFEOS/DOCUMENTATION/ISA/ISAFormat.md`, and enforcement in `hooks/`. `LIFEOS/RULES/SelfHealing.md` says where a new fix belongs.
